The post Nace AI Releases Drex for Search for AI Agents: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus With 12.6 Search Calls appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Nace AI has released Drex for Search , which brings its Drex decision models to document search. Drex for Search is a retrieval layer that helps people and agents find evidence. Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode call it through CLI, SDKs, MCP or REST. In Nace’s evaluation, it scores 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, using 12.6 search calls per question. TL;DR Size: a hosted search system built to search over 1M+ files. It pairs with an answering model such as GPT-5, Gemini 3.5 Flash or Qwen 27B. Runs on: Nace’s managed cloud, a dedicated cloud, your own AWS or Azure account, or on-prem and air-gapped. Performance: ranked #1 or #2 on 3 of 4 public leaderboards, per Nace. Best: 77.5% R@1 on VisDocAgentBench, 10 points above Claude Opus 5 (67.5%). What did Nace AI release? Nace AI frames search as a series of decisions. Drex for Search applies its Drex models to those decisions. Drex scores given options with a calibrated probability each, in 1 forward pass. That makes it cheap enough for every agent step. The release targets classic RAG, which Nace sums up as chunk, embed, top-k, hope. The pipeline breaks in 3 cases: the answer sits in a table on page 23 the answer needs 2 hops across files the answer is inside a scanned PDF How does Drex for Search work inside an agent? Nace describes 3 steps: Classify: Before any search runs, Drex decides if the question needs a quick lookup or an agent. The agent route reads documents and queries tables. Squeeze: Drex walks the workspace level by level: folder, file, section, page. Inside a sheet, it narrows to table and column. Each level keeps only what can hold the answer. Answer: Only the kept pages and tables reach the LLM. The answer cites the file and page. Depth is fixed, so Nace says a million files take as many steps as a thousand. How much does it help coding agents? Nace AI tested 9 agent and model pairs on OfficeQA Pro , a 133-question benchmark over U.S. Treasury Bulletins. Key highlights: 6% more answers right, 62% fewer steps, 56% fewer tokens, and 2.3x faster. The post vLLM Semantic Router Releases d3-ultra: A 27B Open Multimodal Decision Model appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The vLLM Semantic Router team has released d3-ultra , a 27B multimodal decision model under Apache-2.0. The d3-ultra decision model does not generate text. It reads an input once and returns a probability for every answer to every question. For developers, that means routing, classification, visual grounding and video checks from 1 open-weight call. TL;DR Size: 26.09B parameters (dense, including a 0.46B vision encoder); 131,072 tokens of context per question. Runs on: tested on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with BF16 weights; no official quantized variant is listed yet. Performance: highest SR-Text score of the 6 decision models in the team’s own private test. Best: 97.8 on SR-Text tools and automation (chance-corrected accuracy). Worst: 54.6% on SR-Box (9 domains), 5.0 points below its sibling d3-turbo. What is d3-ultra? d3-ultra is a System One decision model from vLLM Semantic Router that answers typed questions with probabilities. It is the newest member of Decision 3.0 , a family that spans 0.6B to 27B. You send a state (text or JSON, plus images or videos) and a set of questions. Each question has a type: Choice: pick 1 of several options. Yes / No: return the probability of yes. Score: rate on a scale. Box: locate something in an image or a video moment. Track: follow a target across a whole video. Images can also sit inside questions and options. A quiz can show a photo, then offer 4 etchings as answers. How does d3-ultra work? The core idea is state once . The model reads the input once per request and answers every question from that single read. The config shows a Qwen3.5-architecture backbone with 64 layers. 48 are linear-attention layers and 16 are full-attention layers. The card does not name its base checkpoint. vLLM’s recipe says the sibling d3 was trained from Qwen3.8-27B. Box answers always return exactly 1 box with a confidence. A confidence near 0 means the target is not in the picture. Questions over 131,072 tokens fail with max_length_exceeded ; nothing is silently truncated. How does d3-ultra perform on benchmarks? The research team compares d3-ultra with GLiDE V1.2 , d1-ultra, d3-turbo, d3 and Jev 1.14 on 2 in-house tests. SR-Text has 10,411 text requests with 73,495 questions. Most recreate skills from 34 public benchmarks with new items. Another 4,896 questions come from 43 new task families, like SQL checks and ticket routing. Scores are chance-corrected: 0 is chance, 100 is perfect. d3-ultra: 87.2 GLiDE V1.2: 85.1 d1-ultra: 83.4 d3-turbo: 83.1 d3: 81.4 Jev 1.14: 73.1 d3-ultra leads every area except arts and human taste. There, d1-ultra scores 90.8 against 89.6, within the margin of error. SR-Box has 5,678 Box questions on 4,984 images across 10 domains. A box counts as correct at IoU 0.5 or higher. d3-ultra scores 58.2% over 10 domains and 54.6% over 9. d3-turbo scores 60.0% and 59.6%. Jev 1.14 scores 45.7% and 46.9%. The team says d3-turbo stays stronger on natural images, while d3-ultra leads on charts. Latency: on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with AutoModel, 1 question about a photo takes 304 ms. 255 questions take 2.16 s, about 7.3 ms per extra question. How do you deploy d3-ultra? There are 4 routes: Transformers: AutoModel.from_pretrained("vllm-sr/d3-ultra", trust_remote_code=True) with transformers==5.17.0 . The optional flash-linear-attention package adds fast GPU kernels. vLLM Semantic Router Engine: vllm-sr serve -e vllm-sr/d3-ultra , added in PR #5449 on October 25, 2026. Free API: the card says decision.vllm-sr.ai serves d3-ultra, with a free key. Demo: the official Hugging Face Space . d3-ultra vs GLiDE V1.2, d1-ultra, Jev 1.14 and d3-turbo Feature d3-ultra d3-turbo GLiDE V1.2 d1-ultra Jev 1.14 Developer vLLM Semantic Router vLLM Semantic Router Fastino Labs Liquid AI TypeSafe Parameters 26.09B 26.09B 26B Not disclosed Not disclosed Context per question 131,072 32,768 default; 131,072 with long_context 40,000 default 32,768 262,144 Weights / license Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Fastino Community License Hosted only Hosted only, proprietary Inputs Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images Text, images Text, images Box / track Box + track Box + track No No Box only SR-Text (self-reported by vLLM-SR) 87.2 83.1 85.1 83.4 73.1 SR-Box, 10 domains 58.2% 60.0% Not supported Not supported 45.7% Public index score Submitted, not yet on board 70.2 Jev DI (own estimate) 71.5 Decision Index 0.4.1 65 AA Decision Index 57 AA Decision Index Price Free API, self-host Free API, self-host $0.04 / M input $0.042 / M input $0.042 / M input Key Takeaways d3-ultra is a 27B Apache-2.0 decision model that never generates text. It reads input once: 255 questions about 1 photo take 2.16 s. It tops the team’s SR-Text test at 87.2, ahead of GLiDE V1.2 at 85.1. It trails d3-turbo on Box grounding: 58.2% vs 60.0%. It reads text, images and video once, then returns probabilities for every answer, scoring 87.2 on the team’s SR-Text test. The post vLLM Semantic Router Releases d3-ultra: A 27B Open Multimodal Decision Model appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The vLLM Semantic Router team has released d3-ultra , a 27B multimodal decision model under Apache-2.0. The d3-ultra decision model does not generate text. It reads an input once and returns a probability for every answer to every question. For developers, that means routing, classification, visual grounding and video checks from 1 open-weight call. TL;DR Size: 26.09B parameters (dense, including a 0.46B vision encoder); 131,072 tokens of context per question. Runs on: tested on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with BF16 weights; no official quantized variant is listed yet. Performance: highest SR-Text score of the 6 decision models in the team’s own private test. Best: 97.8 on SR-Text tools and automation (chance-corrected accuracy). Worst: 54.6% on SR-Box (9 domains), 5.0 points below its sibling d3-turbo. What is d3-ultra? d3-ultra is a System One decision model from vLLM Semantic Router that answers typed questions with probabilities. It is the newest member of Decision 3.0 , a family that spans 0.6B to 27B. You send a state (text or JSON, plus images or videos) and a set of questions. Each question has a type: Choice: pick 1 of several options. Yes / No: return the probability of yes. Score: rate on a scale. Box: locate something in an image or a video moment. Track: follow a target across a whole video. Images can also sit inside questions and options. A quiz can show a photo, then offer 4 etchings as answers. How does d3-ultra work? The core idea is state once . The model reads the input once per request and answers every question from that single read. The config shows a Qwen3.5-architecture backbone with 64 layers. 48 are linear-attention layers and 16 are full-attention layers. The card does not name its base checkpoint. vLLM’s recipe says the sibling d3 was trained from Qwen3.8-27B. Box answers always return exactly 1 box with a confidence. A confidence near 0 means the target is not in the picture. Questions over 131,072 tokens fail with max_length_exceeded ; nothing is silently truncated. How does d3-ultra perform on benchmarks? The research team compares d3-ultra with GLiDE V1.2 , d1-ultra, d3-turbo, d3 and Jev 1.14 on 2 in-house tests. SR-Text has 10,411 text requests with 73,495 questions. Most recreate skills from 34 public benchmarks with new items. Another 4,896 questions come from 43 new task families, like SQL checks and ticket routing. Scores are chance-corrected: 0 is chance, 100 is perfect. d3-ultra: 87.2 GLiDE V1.2: 85.1 d1-ultra: 83.4 d3-turbo: 83.1 d3: 81.4 Jev 1.14: 73.1 d3-ultra leads every area except arts and human taste. There, d1-ultra scores 90.8 against 89.6, within the margin of error. SR-Box has 5,678 Box questions on 4,984 images across 10 domains. A box counts as correct at IoU 0.5 or higher. d3-ultra scores 58.2% over 10 domains and 54.6% over 9. d3-turbo scores 60.0% and 59.6%. Jev 1.14 scores 45.7% and 46.9%. The team says d3-turbo stays stronger on natural images, while d3-ultra leads on charts. Latency: on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with AutoModel, 1 question about a photo takes 304 ms. 255 questions take 2.16 s, about 7.3 ms per extra question. How do you deploy d3-ultra? There are 4 routes: Transformers: AutoModel.from_pretrained("vllm-sr/d3-ultra", trust_remote_code=True) with transformers==5.17.0 . The optional flash-linear-attention package adds fast GPU kernels. vLLM Semantic Router Engine: vllm-sr serve -e vllm-sr/d3-ultra , added in PR #5449 on October 25, 2026. Free API: the card says decision.vllm-sr.ai serves d3-ultra, with a free key. Demo: the official Hugging Face Space . d3-ultra vs GLiDE V1.2, d1-ultra, Jev 1.14 and d3-turbo Feature d3-ultra d3-turbo GLiDE V1.2 d1-ultra Jev 1.14 Developer vLLM Semantic Router vLLM Semantic Router Fastino Labs Liquid AI TypeSafe Parameters 26.09B 26.09B 26B Not disclosed Not disclosed Context per question 131,072 32,768 default; 131,072 with long_context 40,000 default 32,768 262,144 Weights / license Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Fastino Community License Hosted only Hosted only, proprietary Inputs Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images Text, images Text, images Box / track Box + track Box + track No No Box only SR-Text (self-reported by vLLM-SR) 87.2 83.1 85.1 83.4 73.1 SR-Box, 10 domains 58.2% 60.0% Not supported Not supported 45.7% Public index score Submitted, not yet on board 70.2 Jev DI (own estimate) 71.5 Decision Index 0.4.1 65 AA Decision Index 57 AA Decision Index Price Free API, self-host Free API, self-host $0.04 / M input $0.042 / M input $0.042 / M input Key Takeaways d3-ultra is a 27B Apache-2.0 decision model that never generates text. It reads input once: 255 questions about 1 photo take 2.16 s. It tops the team’s SR-Text test at 87.2, ahead of GLiDE V1.2 at 85.1. It trails d3-turbo on Box grounding: 58.2% vs 60.0%. All benchmark numbers are self-reported on private test sets. Check out the model card , the GitHub repo , the Decision 3.0 collection and the Hugging Face Space . The 3B model parses books, filings and reports of hundreds of pages in one request. Its core change is SR-SWA, a sparse attention scheme that keeps per-step decoding cost nearly flat. Weights ship under the MIT license , with code on GitHub . TL;DR Size: 3.34B parameters . Active parameters not disclosed. Max position length 131,072 tokens. Runs on: 1 CUDA GPU in BF16. Baidu tested on an NVIDIA A800-80GB. BF16 weights total about 6.7 GB. Performance: first place on both multi-page benchmarks Baidu tested, against 9 other models (self-reported). Best: 77.1 overall on MarathonDocBench (hundreds of pages). The next model, Kimi-K3, scores 33.7. Worst: 48.2 on heading hierarchy (TEDS) on MarathonDocBench, its lowest sub-score. The post Mirendil Launches Fern 0.1, Its First Model, With 10M-Token Context appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Mirendil has released Fern , its first AI model. Mirendil Fern is a from-scratch coding model with a context window of up to 10M tokens. Mirendil explains how that equals about 23 MB of code, or roughly half a million lines. That is a codebase on the scale of Megatron-LM, held in context at once. Fern 0.1 is the first version, built from Mirendil-Base after a short round of post-training. For developers, its like, you load a whole repo, a full training log or days of agent traces at once. TL;DR Size: 0.1 to 0.5T parameters (exact count and active params not disclosed); context up to 10M tokens. Runs on: Hosted early access only; no open weights or quantized builds announced. Performance: Strong long-context retrieval, mid-pack agentic coding versus open-weight models, well behind frontier models. Best: 100% on RULER single-needle retrieval at every length from 32K to 10M tokens (base model). Worst: 6.1% on Terminal Bench 4.0, versus 66.4% for Claude Opus 5.5 in Mirendil’s own table. What is Mirendil Fern? Fern is a language model from Mirendil , an AI R&D lab. Fern is aimed at AI R&D work, not general chat. Mirendil lists 6 target uses: Working across larger codebases Agentic coding that runs commands until tests pass Research code: training loops, data pipelines and evaluations Debugging training runs from long logs and stack traces Reading full agent or training traces end to end Auditing pretraining shards for duplicates, contamination and junk How was Fern built? Fern sits on Mirendil-Base , which Mirendil says one researcher pretrained in 3.5 months. Total compute was under $10M, including experiments, agent token spend and data processing. AI agents wrote over 99% of the code. The researcher chose what to try and when to intervene. Training data came only from public sources: GitHub, public code, web pages and public datasets. Mirendil says it used no distillation, no synthetic data and no licensed data. The code was written from scratch on PyTorch and JAX. Fern is the smallest of 3 planned models. Mirendil-Base-Large (0.5 to 2T parameters) is over 80% through pretraining. Mirendil-Base-XL (2 to 10T) is over 20% through. Does longer context actually help? Mirendil tested next-token prediction on its own repositories, concatenated into a 42.9 MB stream. It measured cross-entropy in bits per byte, where lower is better. Window sizes here are measured in bytes, not tokens. Fern’s loss fell from 0.246 at a 32K-byte window to 0.155 at 16M and 23M bytes. The other models were scored up to about 1M tokens, their advertised limit. At a 1M-byte window, Kimi-K3 scored 0.140 and Fern 0.165. So Fern is not the best predictor at equal context. Its advantage is that the curve keeps going past where others stop. How does Fern score on RULER? RULER is a standard long-context benchmark. Mirendil ran 5 RULER tasks on Mirendil-Base, the pre-post-training model. It used greedy decoding, thinking off and exact string matching. Multi-hop reasoning drops to 45% at 10M. Each 10M cell uses only 20 examples, versus 100 elsewhere. Mirendil says broader long-context results are coming. How does Fern 0.1 do on agentic benchmarks? This kind of egalitarianism seems unusual given that startup prospectuses usually show a founding CEO with a much larger relative stake compared to co-founders. The company’s co-founders include Dario Amodei , Daniela Amodei , Tom Brown , Jack Clark , Jared Kaplan , Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah . Anthropic’s risk factors take up 93 pages of its IPO filing So, is investing in Anthropic a risky bet? Anthropic certainly seems to think so. The company’s IPO prospectus contains a staggering 93 pages of risk factors. They start at page 27 and end on page 120. Some are pretty mundane. For instance, the company is concerned that slower revenue growth could potentially constrain its ability to fund frontier AI development and attract and retain top talent. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders. Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud . She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison. Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court. Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research . The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction. Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud Kyle Jeziorski of Founder Shield. The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability. Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred: LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.” Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth. Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue. Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own. Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest? Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims. An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout. Where D&O coverage may stop Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends. As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage. Three policy provisions deserve attention: The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions. Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted. Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances. D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 26 Oct 2026 20:13:12 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Crunchbase Data Shows Q3 Robotics Startup Funding Jumps 185% As US And China Lead Physical AI Push https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-us-china-robotics-startup-funding-jumps-physical-ai-push/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:00:53 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94284 Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1 . It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year. China and the US lead The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested. The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics , a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics , which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round. In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick ’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI , which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain. Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics , which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence. Building out the data and model layer “We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen , co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord , a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month. The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said. Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen. We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted. More winners Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others. Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year. “There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen. Miss it in bad faith, and the penalty can reach twice the deposit. That deadline doesn’t care whether the letter was supposed to come from a person or a piece of software. Either way, someone will answer for it. I think about this a lot. At my company, Get Covered , we now run 16 AI agents across more than 3 million rental units. When we built them, the technical questions turned out to be the easier ones. The harder question, for each agent, was actually who it reports to. Rick Folgmann, COO at Get Covered. Most companies are about to face that same question, and few are ready for it. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 23% of companies use agentic AI at least moderately today, and 74% expect to within two years. Gartner , meanwhile, has predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. Those numbers make a case for running agents the way you would run staff in a regulated job, with written rules, a defined scope, a manager and a regular review. Here is what has worked for us, and what I would advise any decision-maker to focus on when it comes to scaling. Start with work that already has a rulebook The best early candidates for agents are tasks where the rules already exist somewhere outside anyone’s head: a statute, a contract clause, an insurance requirement in a vendor agreement. Take vendor certificates of insurance. Across the industry, property teams spend roughly three hours per property every week chasing those documents by email. The work is tedious, however at the same time, it is completely specified. Assignments like these give decision-makers two advantages. First, the agent has something objective to check its output against, and second, your team can audit the result without debating judgment calls. McKinsey ‘s most recent State of AI research found that the small group of companies seeing significant bottom-line returns from AI, about 6% of respondents, were nearly 3x as likely to have fundamentally redesigned their workflows. In my experience, that redesign starts with writing the rule down. If a new hire couldn’t follow your description of a decision on the person’s first day, an agent won’t follow it either. Set autonomy by workflow Tech execs I speak with often ask whether an AI system is autonomous, as if that were a fixed property of the product. In practice, the same agent should run with different levels of freedom depending on what it touches. At Get Covered, we configure each agent on different levels. For instance, a reminder to a vendor whose certificate expires next month can go out automatically. A response to a resident who has requested an emotional support animal never does.
